name: Karlskrona
title: Karlskrona Thickness Measurement | Ferries, Cable Ships, Cargo
description: Thickness measurement in Karlskrona for ro-pax ferries to Gdynia, cable-laying ships at the NKT piers, cargo and cruise ships: deck, tank and hull UTM.
h1: Ship Gauging in Karlskrona for Gdynia Ferries, Cable-Laying Vessels and Cargo Ships
intro: Karlskrona, built across islands in the Blekinge archipelago, is the Swedish Navy's main base and a UNESCO World Heritage naval town, but its commercial port keeps busy in its own right. Stena Line ro-pax ferries sail from Verkö to Gdynia, cable-laying ships load high-voltage cable at the NKT piers, and general cargo and cruise ships use the Verkö quays and the merchant harbour. Atlantis works on the merchant ships calling here, with a team travelling from India to the vessel for every job.

highlights.p: The ferries to Gdynia berth at Verkö, east of the town, and carry lorries, cars and passengers across the southern Baltic. Vehicle decks, ramps and doors take the wear, and gauging is planned for time alongside between crossings or brought into the docking programme.

highlights.h: Cable-laying ships at the NKT piers
highlights.p: Cable-laying vessels come to load high-voltage subsea cable made at the NKT factory. A loading stay is usually longer than a cargo call, which gives time to gauge cable-carousel foundations, tank structure and deck plating, and to crack-test highly loaded welds.

Pilotage into Karlskrona runs in daylight, with arrivals expected well before sunset and departures timed accordingly. In midwinter that shortens the working day for ship movements, so a team's schedule is set around the confirmed berthing time rather than the planned one.

port.h: Karlskrona's archipelago port: naval town, ferry route and cable quays
p: Karlskrona was founded in the late seventeenth century as a naval base, and the city still spreads across a cluster of islands linked by bridges, with fairways threading between skerries towards the open Baltic. Ships approach from the south, pick up the pilot at the boarding position off the approach and follow the channel in; the Swedish Maritime Administration's rules for the port call for two pilots on the larger ships, keep visibility and wind limits for the merchant harbour, and confine pilotage to daylight hours. Anchorage is available at an outer position, in the roads and in the inner roads, while some areas near the naval base, including one between Aspö and Tjurkö, are closed to anchoring. The naval presence shapes the archipelago in ways a visitor notices quickly, from restricted areas to the warships alongside in the naval harbour.

Commercial traffic is concentrated in a few places. The ferry terminal at Verkö serves Stena Line's ro-pax route to Gdynia, and the Verkö quays next to it handle general cargo and cable. The NKT high-voltage cable factory has its own piers and quay where cable-laying vessels load long lengths of subsea cable for interconnectors and offshore wind farms. Cruise ships and passenger vessels use the merchant harbour close to the town centre, mainly in summer. Saab Kockums' shipyard, which builds and maintains naval vessels including submarines, occupies its own part of the port, and the naval harbour is reserved for the navy's own ships. Most merchant ships calling are therefore ferries, cable ships, general cargo vessels and cruise ships, a mix that gives Karlskrona a different inspection profile from the cargo ports of western Blekinge.

The Blekinge archipelago is sheltered, and in a severe winter its inner waters can freeze; the Swedish Maritime Administration then provides icebreaking assistance and may set ice-class restrictions for the port. Ice or not, winter means short days, which combined with daylight-only pilotage limits when ships move. The gauging requests that come from Karlskrona reflect its fleets. Ferry operators want vehicle decks, doors and piping measured before dockings, cable-ship owners want the structure beneath their cable systems checked during loading stays, and general cargo and cruise operators occasionally need condition readings while a ship is alongside for longer than usual. Cable ships in particular may return several times during an installation project, each time for a fresh load, so a gauging programme can be spread across visits and recorded against one plan.

facilities.h: Where merchant ships are gauged in Karlskrona
p: Gauging in Karlskrona is done afloat. The Gdynia ferries lie at the Verkö ferry berth between crossings, long enough for targeted work on vehicle decks, voids and machinery piping when the crew releases the spaces. Cable-laying vessels at the NKT piers are often alongside for an extended loading period, and once the loading plan is known, parts of the deck, cable-tank structure and machinery spaces can be released for measurement around the cable operations. General cargo ships at Verkö 1 and 2 and cruise ships in the merchant harbour are worked under the usual arrangements of the terminal and the ship.

Karlskrona's shipyard is a naval yard, so merchant ships calling here normally dock elsewhere. The Gdynia ferries can use ship-repair yards in the Gdynia and Gdańsk area at the other end of their route, and cable ships and cargo vessels dock wherever their owners have arrangements around the Baltic and North Sea. Readings taken in Karlskrona feed the docking specification, and our team can travel to the yard to complete the programme.
list: Verkö ferry berth — vehicle-deck, ramp, bow and stern door and machinery piping gauging on the Gdynia ro-pax ships between crossings.
NKT cable piers and quay — deck plating, cable-carousel and tensioner foundations and cable-tank structure gauged on cable-laying vessels during loading stays.
Verkö 1 and 2 general cargo berths — hold, hatch coaming and ballast tank readings on general cargo and project ships.
Merchant harbour — condition and piping gauging on cruise and passenger ships alongside near the town centre.
Outer anchorage and the roads — limited launch-borne work on ships waiting to berth, in daylight and suitable weather.
The ship's docking yard — often in Poland for the Gdynia ferries — with the team travelling on to complete the scope.

context.h: Naval surroundings, port state control and ferry rules
p: The Swedish Transport Agency carries out port state control in Karlskrona under the Paris MoU, and the Gdynia ro-pax ships also fall under the EU regime of inspections for ro-pax ships in regular service, which looks closely at vehicle-deck structure, doors and hull condition. As the crossing links two EU ports, its emissions are counted in full under the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, and the ships calling here carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. The naval base adds its own constraints. Parts of the archipelago are military protected areas, so access routes, anchoring and the photography of surroundings can be restricted; inspection photographs taken on board are normally confined to the structure being reported, and the agent confirms any local conditions before the team arrives.

Cable-laying ships bring a different set of structural questions. Their carousels and cable tanks place very large, concentrated loads on decks and internal structure, tensioners and chutes are bolted or welded to foundations that see repeated loading and unloading, and many of these ships have been converted from other types, so original and added structure meet at welded interfaces. Thickness readings around those foundations, together with magnetic particle testing of the welds, give owners a record of condition before a long installation campaign. For ferries and other ships trading north in winter, the Finnish-Swedish ice class and the condition of the ice belt remain a separate gauging item.

jobs.h: Thickness measurement jobs we see in Karlskrona
jobs.p: Karlskrona jobs are few in type but distinctive. Ferry work concentrates on vehicle decks, ramps, doors and piping and is fitted around the Gdynia timetable; cable-ship work is planned around the loading programme agreed with the cable factory; cargo and cruise work follows the terminal's arrangements. Every scope is agreed with the superintendent before the team travels, and the agent confirms berthing times against the daylight pilotage rules so that the team arrives when the ship does. Results reach the superintendent the same day, and where a ship is heading for a docking soon afterwards, the readings are passed to the yard's planners as well. Examples include:
list: Vehicle-deck plating, drainage gutters and stern ramp structure on a Gdynia ro-pax ship, measured during time alongside at Verkö before her docking.
Cable-carousel foundation, surrounding deck plating and stiffeners gauged on a cable-laying vessel during a loading stay at the NKT piers, with weld crack testing.
Machinery-space sea-water and fuel piping on a ferry, to decide which runs are renewed at the next docking in Poland.
Hold, tank-top and hatch coaming readings on a general cargo ship at Verkö, for an owner's condition record.
Condition gauging of selected ballast tanks and piping on a passenger ship alongside in the merchant harbour.

logistics: Copenhagen Airport is the main international arrival point, with regional trains running through Skåne and Blekinge to Karlskrona. Ronneby Airport, close by to the west, has domestic flights, and Kalmar is another option. The ferry terminal, the cable piers and the merchant harbour are ISPS-controlled, and the cable factory sets its own site rules, so the agent registers the team's names in advance and arranges passes. The technicians travel from India on Schengen visas, and the agent keeps us informed of berthing changes caused by weather or daylight limits.

faqs.q: Can a cable-laying vessel be gauged while she loads cable at the NKT piers?
faqs.a: Often, yes. A loading stay usually lasts longer than a cargo call, and spaces away from the cable path can be released once the loading plan is fixed. Deck plating, carousel and tensioner foundations, cable-tank structure and the machinery spaces are typical items. We agree the sequence with the ship's officers and the cable factory, so measurements never get in the way of the loading.

faqs.q: Can the Gdynia ferries be gauged during their time at Verkö?
faqs.a: A targeted scope can be done while a ferry lies alongside between crossings: vehicle-deck areas the crew can keep clear, voids and machinery piping. Ballast tank work needs tanks emptied, ventilated and certified safe for entry, which is better planned for a lay-over or the docking. We agree the plan with the operator's technical department well in advance.

faqs.q: Does the naval base affect access for a merchant-ship inspection?
faqs.a: It can shape the arrangements. Parts of the archipelago are military protected areas, so anchoring, access routes and photography of the surroundings may be restricted. Merchant terminals such as Verkö, the cable piers and the merchant harbour are reached through the ship's agent in the normal way, and the agent tells us of any local conditions before the team arrives.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Karlskrona for merchant ships?
faqs.a: The shipyard in Karlskrona is a naval yard, so merchant ships usually dock elsewhere. The Gdynia ferries can dock in yards at the Polish end of their route, and other ships go where their owners have arrangements. Readings taken in Karlskrona are tied to the TM plan for use by the yard and class surveyor, and our team can travel to the yard.

faqs.q: How do daylight pilotage rules affect a job in winter?
faqs.a: Ships enter and leave Karlskrona in daylight, so in midwinter a ship may arrive later or sail earlier than its schedule suggests. Work on board is not limited by daylight, but the time the ship spends alongside can shift. We plan the team's dates with some margin and confirm the berthing time with the agent before travelling to the port.
